sermon:
A man is left behind on an island. Paul sailed on; Titus stayed. Crete was not a vacation post. It was a hard field with a bad reputation, and the work Paul handed his younger colleague was the unglamorous labor of putting a house back in order. "This is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town as I directed you" (Titus 1:5). What remained. The phrase admits that the work was not finished, that churches had been planted but not stabilized, that the gospel had landed but the leadership had not yet been set.

The whole of Titus 1 turns on a single conviction: a church without proven leaders is a church without defense.

**Character Is the Qualification**

Paul lists what an elder must be, and the list is striking for what it is not. It is not a list of gifts. It is not a measure of charisma, eloquence, or crowd. It is a measure of life. Above reproach. Husband of one wife. Children who are not wild or disobedient. Not arrogant, not quick-tempered, not a drunkard, not violent, not greedy for gain. Then the positive turn: hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, disciplined. Only at the end does competence appear, and even then it is competence rooted in fidelity: "He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it" (Titus 1:9).

Notice the order. The man is examined before the teacher is approved. We have often reversed this. We have asked whether a man can fill a room before we asked whether he can be trusted in an empty one. We have promoted ability and then been surprised by the wreckage of character. Paul does not allow the inversion. The teaching only carries weight because the life beneath it carries weight. I have to sit inside this myself, because it is easier to prepare a sermon than to govern a temper, easier to be right than to be holy.

**The Empty Talk Must Be Silenced**

The reason for proven elders becomes plain in the second half of the chapter. "For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party. They must be silenced, since they are upsetting whole families by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach" (Titus 1:10-11). Whole families. The damage was not abstract. It reached into households, unsettled them, taught them what was false, and did it for money.

Paul does not counsel polite dialogue here. He says silence them. He even quotes a Cretan source about the failings of his own people and then adds, "This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith" (Titus 1:13). The sharpness is not cruelty. It is mercy aimed at restoration, that they may be sound. But it is sharp. A shepherd who will not confront the wolf is not gentle; he is asleep. The closing verse exposes the real fault line: "They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works" (Titus 1:16). The problem was never merely doctrinal. It was a life that contradicted the confession.

**The Grace Beneath the Order**

Why does any of this matter to a Savior on a cross? Because Paul opens the letter naming himself "a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, for the sake of the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness, in hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began" (Titus 1:1-2). God who never lies. Against a culture of liars and empty talkers, the gospel stands as the word of the One who cannot deceive. The order in the house is not bureaucracy. It is the protection of a promise made before the ages, guarded now in ordinary towns by ordinary men whose lives have been remade by grace. The same grace that will, in the next chapter, train a people to live well.

The house is put in order so the truth can stand. The truth stands because God does not lie.

Character qualifies. Empty talk must stop.

Begin with the word that governs the chapter: adorn. "That in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior" (Titus 2:10). It is a strange thing to say about doctrine. We expect doctrine to be defended, explained, perhaps argued. Paul says it can be made beautiful, and the people who make it beautiful are not theologians but the plainest members of the church doing the plainest things well. The whole chapter is built on the conviction that what we believe is shown in how we live, and that a watching world reads the gospel in the conduct of those who claim it.

**Sound Doctrine Reaches Every Kind of Person**

Paul moves through the household like a man walking room to room. Older men: sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled, sound in faith and love and steadfastness. Older women: reverent, not slanderers, not slaves to drink, teachers of what is good, so that they may train the younger women to love their husbands and children. Younger men: self-controlled, and Titus himself a model of good works. Slaves: submissive, not pilfering, showing good faith.

The sweep is the point. There is no one in the room too old to be taught, no one too young, no one too low. Sound doctrine does not float above ordinary life in a study; it descends into marriages and workplaces and the management of a temper. We are tempted to think the gospel is for the dramatic moments, the deathbed, the crisis, the conversion. Paul aims it at the Tuesday. He aims it at how a young wife speaks to her husband, how an old man carries his years, how a worker handles money that is not his. I feel the rebuke. It is possible to hold sound doctrine and be a difficult person to live beside, and Paul will not let that stand.

**Grace Is a Teacher**

Then the chapter opens to its center, and the reason for all the conduct becomes clear. "For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age" (Titus 2:11-12). Training us. Grace is not only pardon. Grace is a teacher, and the curriculum is the renunciation of everything that was killing us and the slow learning of a different way to be human.

This dismantles a lie we keep telling ourselves, that grace is the permission slip for staying as we are. It is the opposite. The same grace that forgives the drunkard is the grace that teaches him to set the bottle down. The same grace that receives the slanderer is the grace that trains her tongue. Grace does not lower the standard. It supplies the power and the motive to meet it, and it does so by teaching us to say no. Self-control is not white-knuckled willpower in this chapter. It is the fruit of having been taught by a grace that has already appeared.

**The Appearing That Anchors It All**

And grace teaches us to wait. "Waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works" (Titus 2:13-14). Two appearings frame the Christian life. He has appeared in grace at the manger and the cross; he will appear in glory at the end. We live in the space between, and that space is not idle. He gave himself to purify a people, his own possession, zealous for good. The good works are not how we earn him. They are the evidence that he has already bought us.

So the old man's dignity, the young wife's love, the worker's honesty, these are not religious extras. They are the doctrine made beautiful, the answer to the One who gave himself for us. We adorn the gospel because we belong to the One who appeared, and we wait because he appears again.

Grace teaches us to say no.

Paul opens the last chapter pointing at the door. The church is not a fortress; it lives in a society, under rulers, among neighbors who do not believe. "Remind them to be submissive to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work, to speak evil of no one, to avoid quarreling, to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people" (Titus 3:1-2). Ready for every good work. Gentle toward all. That is a high bar, and Paul knows it is a bar these people could not clear on their own, because he immediately reminds them of what they used to be.

**Remember What You Were**

"For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures, passing our days in malice and envy, hated by others and hating one another" (Titus 3:3). We ourselves. Paul does not stand above the indictment; he stands inside it. The list is ugly and honest. Foolish. Disobedient. Hating and hated. Before we are tempted to feel superior to the difficult neighbor, the rude official, the quarrelsome relative, Paul holds up a mirror. That was us. The gentleness he commands toward all people is the gentleness of those who remember they were rescued from the same pit.

This is where so much of our hardness comes from. We forget. We treat our own goodness as native to us and other people's failures as native to them. Paul refuses the amnesia. The honest Christian is not the one who has never been foolish; it is the one who has not forgotten that he was.

**Saved by Mercy, Not by Merit**

Then the great reversal, the hinge of the whole letter. "But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit" (Titus 3:4-5). Not because of works done by us. Every door to boasting is shut. We did not climb out of the pit; we were lifted. The washing of regeneration is not something we performed on ourselves; it is something done to us, the renewal of the Spirit poured out richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs.

Here again is the appearing. The goodness and loving kindness of God appeared, and it saved. This is the same grace from chapter two, now traced to its root: mercy, not merit. And mercy received does something. It does not leave a person passive. Paul says he insists on these things "so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works" (Titus 3:8). The mercy that asks nothing of us to be saved makes everything of us once we are.

**Done With What Profits No One**

So the chapter ends by clearing away what wastes a saved life. "But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable and worthless" (Titus 3:9). Unprofitable. Worthless. The same energy that should fuel good works gets burned up in arguments that go nowhere, and Paul has no patience for it. A divisive person, after two warnings, is to be let go. The point is not coldness; it is stewardship. A people saved by mercy and made ready for good work have no time for quarrels that profit no one.

I feel the weight of that. It is easier to be right in an argument than to be useful to a neighbor, easier to defend my position than to do the good work in front of me. The chapter will not let me hide there. We were saved by mercy precisely so that we could be poured out for others as he was poured out for us.

He saved us. Now be ready.
